name: Xanthomonas bacterial leaf spot
summary: A documented bacterial leaf spot of hemp in which small water-soaked lesions progress to approximately 1–2 mm necrotic centers surrounded by comparatively broad yellow halos; images can support triage but cannot distinguish the bacterium from fungal or abiotic look-alikes.
stages: growth stage not established in cannabis-specific primary evidence
indicators: Small water-soaked leaf spots before necrosis develops
Necrotic centers approximately 1–2 mm in diameter
Discrete lesions with a halo wider than the necrotic center
Focal spotting rather than a whole-leaf nutrient-mobility gradient
exclusions: White surface colonies, fungal fruiting structures, or diagnostic spores support a fungal cause
Fine stippling, webbing, or organisms on the leaf underside support arthropod feeding
Damage follows spray droplets, contact points, or a documented chemical application and does not progress after exposure ends
Symptoms follow a measured older-leaf or younger-leaf nutrient pattern without discrete water-soaked lesions
A plant diagnostic laboratory identifies another pathogen or abiotic cause from a representative active lesion

progression.description: A small water-soaked spot develops in leaf tissue; record both leaf surfaces because general bacterial leaf spots can first be more apparent from below.
The center becomes necrotic at roughly 1–2 mm across while a yellow halo roughly 2–3 mm wide surrounds it, producing a small dark center with a proportionally broad chlorotic border.

Cannabis-specific primary evidence used here does not establish a dependable late-stage coalescence, defoliation, stem, or flower pattern. Do not infer those labels from general-host bacterial leaf-spot images.

lookAlikes: Septoria or other fungal leaf spot
Edema or water-soaking from physiological stress
confirmation: Photograph the whole plant and both sides of several leaves, then capture a scale-referenced close-up showing the necrotic-center and halo dimensions and the distribution of lesions across the canopy.

Submit fresh, recently expanding lesions that include the transition between healthy and affected tissue to a plant diagnostic laboratory; keep samples separate, cool, and dry according to that laboratory’s instructions.

Ask the laboratory to distinguish bacterial from fungal leaf spot and, if a Xanthomonas isolate is recovered, identify it with validated physiological and molecular or sequence-based methods rather than morphology alone.
Microscopic bacterial streaming may support a bacterial differential, but absence of streaming does not exclude bacteria and streaming does not confirm Xanthomonas cannabis to species.
Map reports using the current accepted name Xanthomonas cannabis while retaining Xanthomonas campestris pv. cannabis as a historical synonym for literature and laboratory searches.
immediateActions: Flag the plant and pause movement of cuttings or symptomatic foliage until laboratory triage.
Handle suspect foliage only when dry, avoid splash between plants, and clean hands and tools before moving to unaffected plants.
Keep unconfirmed lesion photographs out of bacterial ground-truth and training sets.
correctivePlan: Base removal, sanitation, and any crop treatment on the confirmed diagnosis and local legal label; a visual bacterial-leaf-spot suspicion is not a treatment prescription.
Inspect nearby plants for comparable small haloed lesions and document whether new lesions appear after splash or handling events without treating that association as proof.
If laboratory results do not recover or identify the bacterium, reopen fungal, arthropod, chemical, and physiological differentials.
prevention: Use documented healthy propagation material and retain lot or mother-plant traceability.
Minimize leaf wetness and splash during routine handling where compatible with the production system.
Disinfect tools and segregate symptomatic material under a written sanitation protocol.
warnings: A photograph or video cannot confirm Xanthomonas cannabis; lesion size and halo geometry are triage features only.
The key symptom measurements come from a historical Japanese hemp report and do not establish current local prevalence, cultivar susceptibility, or production-system risk.
General greenhouse bacterial-leaf-spot guidance is used only for differential diagnosis and handling precautions, not as cannabis-specific epidemiological proof.
No cannabis-specific image or video with verified reuse and automated-training permission was found for this batch; no media was copied or admitted.

sources.title: Bacterial leaf spot of hemp caused by Xanthomonas campestris pv. cannabis in Japan
sources.publisher: Springer Nature on behalf of the Phytopathological Society of Japan
supportedClaims: The cannabis-specific Japanese report described leaf lesions with necrotic centers approximately 1–2 mm in diameter and yellow halos approximately 2–3 mm wide.
Pathological, physiological, and genetic characterization linked the Japanese causal bacterium to the organism historically named Xanthomonas campestris pv. cannabis in Romania.

sources.title: Comparative genomics of a cannabis pathogen reveals insight into the evolution of pathogenicity in Xanthomonas
supportedClaims: Cannabis bacterial leaf spot was described as water-soaked lesions followed by necrosis with a yellow halo.
The study sequenced two geographically distinct strains previously isolated from symptomatic cannabis tissue in Japan and Romania and proposed the species name Xanthomonas cannabis.

sources.title: Species: Xanthomonas cannabis
sources.organization: List of Prokaryotic names with Standing in Nomenclature (LPSN)
supportedClaims: Xanthomonas cannabis (ex Severin 1978) McKnight et al. 2026 is the validly published correct species name.
The historical names Xanthomonas campestris pv. cannabis and the 2015 proposed name “Xanthomonas cannabis” are homotypic synonyms; type strain identifiers include ICMP 6570, LMG 9042, and NCPPB 2877.

sources.title: Bacterial Leaf Spot on Greenhouse Ornamentals
supportedClaims: Across greenhouse ornamental hosts, bacterial and fungal leaf spots can be visually confounded; bacterial streaming can support suspicion but may be absent, and diagnosis by a plant disease clinic is recommended.

As general bacterial-leaf-spot precautions rather than cannabis-specific epidemiology, splashing water and handling wet plants can spread bacteria, so suspect plants should be handled dry and separately.
